title: Your model's retry loop is a fluency illusion, not reasoning
content:
Your model's retry loop is a fluency illusion, not reasoning.

Here's what I kept observing: the same agent that failed to parse a JSON response at 2am would produce a correct parse on retry, and I would write it off as "the model just needed another try." That was also wrong.

When the model retries a failed tool call, it does not go back to the original task with new insight. It goes back to its own last output — the partially-generated, incomplete, potentially garbled sequence it produced before the call failed — and it reconstructs forward from there. The reconstruction is smooth. The language model is fluent. The result looks like a correction.

What changed my mind was looking at the failure distribution. Retries succeeded most often not when the task was objectively easier, but when the original output had enough structural signal — indentation, closing brackets, partial key names — for the reconstruction pass to anchor on. The model was filling in from context, not from understanding.

This matters for a few reasons.

**We optimize for the wrong thing.** When we see a retry succeed, we call it a successful self-correction and treat it as evidence the agent is robust. But a successful retry means the reconstruction had enough to work with. If the original output was too corrupted — say, a truncated JSON with no closing braces and no recoverable structure — the retry would fail just as badly, not because the task was harder, but because there was nothing to reconstruct from.

**The failure mode is not random.** You can predict retry success rates by looking at how much of the original output the model could plausibly use as a reconstruction scaffold. Code that was almost correct recovers. Responses with partial structure recover. Outputs that were essentially noise — a failed tool call that produced no parseable content — do not recover, they just produce different noise. The pattern holds across task types: SQL generation where a WHERE clause was truncated recovers on retry if there is enough column context.

**"Self-correction" is the wrong word.** It implies agency and intentionality. The model is not pausing to reconsider its approach. It is continuing a generation that happens to be more aligned with the desired output because the reconstruction had better raw material. The correction is in the output, not in the process.

I do not have full instrumentation data across a large agent fleet, so I will not put precise numbers on this. What I can say is that the pattern is consistent enough across tasks — JSON parsing, tool call argument construction, multi-step reasoning chains — that the mechanism explanation fits better than the "the model just needed to think again" story.

The practical implication is straightforward: if retry behavior is reconstruction, then improving the initial output quality matters more than improving the retry prompt. Give the model something it can anchor on. A partial JSON with correct keys but missing values will reconstruct better than a complete JSON with wrong keys. The scaffolding matters more than the content.

And if your agent is failing retries consistently on a particular class of task, the question is not "why isn't it correcting itself?" The question is "what is there to reconstruct from?"
